notes.title: Angina: chest pain that comes with effort

lines.text: A 58-year-old man gets tight, squeezing chest pain when climbing stairs. It goes away after 3 minutes of rest.
Pain on exertion, relieved by rest or nitroglycerin within minutes → stable angina.
Pain that is new, more frequent, longer (over 20 min) or comes at rest → unstable angina: treat as an emergency, it can become MI.
Pain at rest or waking from sleep with temporary ST elevation → variant (Prinzmetal) angina from coronary spasm.
Diabetic or elderly patient with ischemia but no pain → silent ischemia; they show fatigue and breathlessness instead.
Troponin and CK-MB are normal in angina, raised in MI. That is how you tell them apart.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Heavy, squeezing pressure behind the sternum, may spread to jaw, neck, arm → typical ischemic pain. Sharp, stabbing pain is not typical.
Pain after a heavy meal, cold exposure, exertion or anger → these raise the heart's oxygen demand.
Stop activity, sit the patient down, give oxygen if saturation is low.
Nitroglycerin 0.4–0.5 mg under the tongue; repeat every 5 minutes, up to 3 doses.
Check BP before each dose: do not give nitroglycerin if systolic BP is 90 mmHg or less.
Pain not gone after 3 doses (15 minutes) → treat as MI: call for help, ECG, aspirin.
Long term: aspirin, beta-blocker (target resting HR 50–60), stop smoking, control BP, sugar, cholesterol, weight.
Nitroglycerin dilates veins → less blood returns to the heart → less work, less oxygen needed. That is also why it drops BP.
Beta-blockers slow the heart → less oxygen demand.
Nitro tablets lose strength: keep in the dark glass bottle, replace every 6 months; a slight sting under the tongue means it is active.
Headache after nitroglycerin is an expected side effect, not a reason to stop it.
Never give nitroglycerin to someone who took sildenafil (Viagra) in the last 24 hours: severe hypotension.
A patient with known angina has chest pain at home. He took one nitroglycerin tablet 5 minutes ago and the pain continues. What should he do?
a. Wait 30 minutes before another tablet ✗: too long; the next dose is due after 5 minutes.
b. Take a second tablet and call for emergency help if pain persists ✓: repeat every 5 minutes up to 3; persistent pain may be MI.
c. Take aspirin and go to sleep ✗: unrelieved pain needs urgent assessment, not rest at home.
d. Take three tablets at once ✗: dangerous drop in BP; doses are spaced 5 minutes apart.

notes.title: Myocardial infarction: the first minutes

lines.text: A 55-year-old smoker has crushing chest pain for 40 minutes, sweating, nausea and fear of dying. Rest and nitroglycerin did not help.
Chest pain over 20–30 minutes, not relieved by rest or nitroglycerin → think MI.
ECG within 10 minutes of arrival; troponin confirms heart muscle damage.
The first 20 minutes are critical; muscle death continues for hours, so speed saves heart muscle.
Most MIs damage the left ventricle → watch for heart failure and shock.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Crushing pain spreading to left arm, jaw or neck + sweating, pallor, nausea → MI.
Women, elderly and diabetics may have only breathlessness, fatigue or nausea.
Low BP, fast weak pulse, cold skin → low cardiac output, risk of cardiogenic shock.
Mild fever and raised WBC after 12–24 hours → normal reaction to dead tissue.
Bed rest, semi-Fowler's position, oxygen if saturation is below 90%, IV line, cardiac monitor.
Aspirin immediately (chewed).
Nitroglycerin sublingual if BP allows.
Morphine 2–4 mg IV if pain continues: relieves pain, anxiety and lowers preload.
Heparin to prevent new clots; thrombolytic (streptokinase) to dissolve the clot in STEMI.
Beta-blocker (atenolol, metoprolol) once stable.
Stay with the patient; calm presence reduces fear and oxygen demand.
Troponin: rises 3–6 h, peaks 10–24 h, stays raised 10–14 days → best marker, also for late arrivals.
CK-MB: rises 4–8 h, peaks 15–24 h, normal by 3–4 days → useful for detecting a new re-infarction.
Myoglobin: rises first (1–3 h), normal in 12 h, but not specific to the heart.
Healing: inflammation settles by 48 h; scar forms in 6–8 weeks.
Thrombolytics are not given in unstable angina, and not with recent bleeding, stroke or surgery.
Do not give IM injections to a possible MI patient: they raise CK and bleed when thrombolytics are given.
Most dangerous early complication: arrhythmia (VF). Keep the patient on a monitor.
A 60-year-old with chest pain for 1 hour has ST elevation on ECG. Which nursing action comes first?
a. Teach about a low-fat diet ✗: teaching waits until the patient is stable.
b. Give aspirin, oxygen if hypoxic, and place on a cardiac monitor ✓: immediate MI care limits damage and detects arrhythmia.
c. Send the patient for a walk to test exercise tolerance ✗: activity increases oxygen demand and worsens infarction.
d. Give an IM analgesic injection ✗: IM injections are avoided in MI; morphine is given IV.

notes.title: Heart failure: left side vs right side

lines.text: A 65-year-old with long-standing hypertension wakes at night breathless, has crackles in both lung bases and swollen ankles.
Left-sided failure → blood backs up into the LUNGS: breathlessness, orthopnea, PND, crackles, frothy sputum.
Right-sided failure → blood backs up into the BODY: raised JVP, leg and sacral edema, big tender liver, ascites, weight gain.
Most common cause of right failure is left failure.
Right failure caused by lung disease (COPD) → cor pulmonale.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Needs several pillows to breathe → orthopnea (left failure).
Wakes 1–5 hours after sleep gasping → paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (left failure).
Weight up 1–2 kg in a day or 2–3 kg in a week → fluid retention, failure worsening.
S3 gallop, fast pulse, confusion, low urine → poor cardiac output.
High-Fowler's (sitting up, legs down) and oxygen when breathless.
Weigh daily: same time, same scale, same clothes.
Record intake and output; restrict salt and fluids as ordered.
Rest with activity spaced out; help with daily care to save energy.
Give diuretics (furosemide), ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker, digoxin as ordered.
With furosemide: check potassium, give potassium-rich foods (banana, orange, potato).
NYHA class I: no symptoms with activity. II: symptoms with ordinary activity. III: with minimal activity. IV: symptoms at rest.
Normal ejection fraction 55–70%; below 40% = systolic failure.
BNP below 100 pg/ml makes heart failure unlikely.
Digoxin: count apical pulse for a full minute; hold if below 60 and report.
Low potassium makes digoxin toxicity more likely. Toxicity signs: nausea, poor appetite, confusion, visual changes, slow pulse.
Give IV furosemide no faster than 20 mg/min (fast push can damage hearing).
A patient with heart failure on furosemide and digoxin complains of nausea, poor appetite and seeing yellow halos. Pulse is 52/min. What should the nurse do first?
a. Give the next digoxin dose ✗: these are digoxin toxicity signs; giving more is dangerous.
b. Hold digoxin and report; check potassium and digoxin level ✓: low K from furosemide makes digoxin toxicity more likely.
c. Give extra furosemide ✗: more diuretic lowers potassium further.
d. Encourage a high-salt diet ✗: salt worsens fluid retention in heart failure.

notes.title: Acute pulmonary edema: lungs filling with fluid

lines.text: A patient with heart failure suddenly becomes very breathless at rest, anxious, sweating, coughing pink frothy sputum. Crackles all over the chest.
Pink frothy sputum + severe breathlessness + crackles → acute pulmonary edema, a life-threatening emergency.
Cause is usually the left ventricle failing (MI, heart failure, mitral stenosis) or fluid overload.
Sit upright with legs hanging down: less blood returns to the heart.
High-flow oxygen.
IV furosemide (fast-acting loop diuretic) to remove fluid.
IV morphine: reduces anxiety, breathing effort and venous return.
Nitroglycerin to reduce preload, if BP allows.
Stop or slow IV fluids; monitor intake, output, saturation and BP closely.
Do not lay this patient flat: it floods the lungs more.
Running IV fluid fast in an elderly or heart patient can cause it: check fluid rate and lungs during infusions.
A patient receiving IV fluids becomes acutely breathless with crackles and pink frothy sputum. What is the first action?
a. Increase the IV rate ✗: more fluid worsens the overload.
b. Stop the infusion, sit the patient upright and give oxygen ✓: removes the cause and eases breathing immediately.
c. Place the patient flat with legs raised ✗: increases venous return and worsens lung congestion.
d. Give a sedative and observe ✗: delays urgent treatment.

notes.title: Cardiac arrest: CPR and what to give

lines.text: A patient on the ward collapses. He does not respond, is not breathing normally, only gasping.
Unresponsive + no normal breathing → cardiac arrest: call for help and start CPR. Gasping is not breathing.
Check pulse no longer than 10 seconds: carotid in adults and children, brachial in infants.
Do not waste time taking BP or listening for heart sounds.
Current order is C-A-B: compressions first, then airway, then breathing.
Shockable rhythms: ventricular fibrillation and pulseless VT → defibrillate. Asystole and PEA are NOT shocked.
Push hard and fast on the centre of the chest: 100–120 per minute, 5–6 cm deep in adults, full recoil.
30 compressions : 2 breaths (one rescuer, any age; two rescuers in children/infants: 15:2).
Attach the defibrillator as soon as it arrives; shock VF/pulseless VT, then resume CPR immediately for 2 minutes.
Epinephrine 1 mg IV every 3–5 minutes.
Amiodarone for VF/VT that persists after shocks.
In PEA/asystole look for reversible causes: 5 H's and 5 T's.
Brain cells start dying after 4–6 minutes without circulation.
VF causes 80–90% of sudden adult cardiac arrests.
5 H's: hypovolemia, hypoxia, hydrogen ion (acidosis), hypo/hyperkalemia, hypothermia.
5 T's: tablets/toxins, tamponade, tension pneumothorax, thrombosis coronary, thrombosis pulmonary.
The order is C-A-B, not A-B-C; give one shock at a time, then 2 minutes of CPR before checking the rhythm again.
Atropine is no longer used for asystole; epinephrine is the drug.
Foreign-body choking in a conscious adult → abdominal thrusts (Heimlich); if they become unconscious → start CPR.
A nurse finds an adult patient unresponsive, not breathing, with no carotid pulse. What should she do first after calling for help?
a. Take the blood pressure ✗: wastes time; absent pulse is enough to act.
b. Start chest compressions at 100–120/min ✓: compressions first keep blood flowing to the brain.
c. Give atropine IV ✗: not a first step and not used for arrest anymore.
d. Look for the cause in the chart ✗: causes are searched during CPR, not before it.

notes.title: Arrhythmias: the ones that matter

lines.text: A patient on a cardiac monitor suddenly shows a chaotic wavy line and becomes unresponsive.
Sinus bradycardia (under 60): treat only if symptomatic → atropine 0.5–1 mg IV.
Sinus tachycardia (over 100): treat the cause (fever, pain, bleeding, anxiety, thyroid).
Atrial fibrillation: irregularly irregular pulse, no P waves → risk of stroke; needs rate control and anticoagulation.
Ventricular fibrillation: chaotic line, no pulse → defibrillate immediately + CPR.
Third-degree (complete) heart block: atria and ventricles beat separately → pacemaker.
Check the patient, not just the monitor: a loose lead can look like VF.
Measure pulse deficit: apical rate minus radial rate (present in AF).
Ask about dizziness and fainting; keep antiarrhythmic levels steady.
A monitor shows ventricular fibrillation. The patient is unresponsive with no pulse. What is the priority?
a. Give atropine ✗: used for symptomatic bradycardia, not VF.
b. Defibrillate and start CPR ✓: VF is a shockable rhythm; shock as soon as possible.
c. Record a 12-lead ECG ✗: wastes critical time.
d. Check the blood pressure ✗: no pulse means no measurable BP; act at once.

notes.title: Cor pulmonale: right heart failure from lung disease

lines.text: A 62-year-old with long-standing COPD now has swollen legs, distended neck veins and an enlarged liver.
Lung disease → low oxygen → pulmonary arteries constrict → right ventricle enlarges and fails.
COPD causes more than half of cases.
Treat the lung problem first; oxygen is the key treatment.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Chronic cough + breathlessness + leg edema + raised JVP + big liver → cor pulmonale.
Hematocrit over 50% → body making extra RBCs because of chronic hypoxia (polycythemia).
Low-flow oxygen guided by saturation (target 88–92% in COPD).
Head of bed up, frequent rest, cluster care.
Salt restriction and diuretics for edema; bronchodilators by nebulizer.
Phlebotomy if hematocrit is 55% or more.
High-flow oxygen in a COPD patient who retains CO2 can make him drowsy (CO2 narcosis). Give controlled oxygen.
A COPD patient has leg edema, raised JVP and hematocrit 57%. Which condition best explains this?
a. Left-sided heart failure from MI ✗: would show mainly lung congestion, not a COPD picture.
b. Cor pulmonale ✓: right heart failure from chronic lung disease; hypoxia raises hematocrit.
c. Iron deficiency anemia ✗: anemia lowers hematocrit.
d. Cardiac tamponade ✗: sudden, with low BP and muffled heart sounds.

notes.title: Valve diseases: which one is it?

lines.text: A 28-year-old woman with a history of rheumatic fever has breathlessness, palpitations and an irregular pulse. A low rumbling diastolic murmur is heard at the apex.
In Ethiopia, the main cause of valve disease in young people is rheumatic heart disease.
Mitral stenosis → left atrium overloaded: breathlessness, atrial fibrillation, hemoptysis, low-pitched diastolic rumble at apex.
Mitral regurgitation → blowing holosystolic murmur at the apex, fatigue and breathlessness.
Aortic stenosis → classic triad: angina, syncope (fainting), breathlessness on exertion; systolic murmur at the right 2nd ICS.
Aortic regurgitation → wide pulse pressure, bounding (water-hammer) pulse, head bobbing, early diastolic murmur.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Irregularly irregular pulse in mitral stenosis → atrial fibrillation: high stroke risk from clots in the atrium.
Fainting on exertion in an older patient → aortic stenosis.
Monitor for heart failure: weight, breath sounds, edema.
Anticoagulants (warfarin) in atrial fibrillation or mechanical valves; watch for bleeding.
Prevent endocarditis and rheumatic fever recurrence: benzathine penicillin as ordered, good dental hygiene.
Aortic stenosis: avoid heavy exertion; report chest pain or fainting.
Listening areas: aortic = right 2nd ICS; pulmonic = left 2nd ICS; Erb's = left 3rd; tricuspid = left 4th; mitral (apex) = left 5th ICS midclavicular.
A young woman with rheumatic heart disease has palpitations, an irregularly irregular pulse and a diastolic rumble at the apex. Which complication should the nurse watch for most?
a. Hypoglycemia ✗: not related to mitral stenosis.
b. Stroke from a clot ✓: AF with mitral stenosis forms clots in the left atrium that travel to the brain.
c. Hyperkalemia ✗: not a feature of valve disease.
d. Hypothyroidism ✗: unrelated.

notes.title: Rheumatic heart disease and infective endocarditis

lines.text: A 12-year-old had a sore throat 3 weeks ago. Now he has fever, painful swollen knees that move from joint to joint, and a new murmur.
Untreated strep throat → 2–4 weeks later rheumatic fever → heart valves scarred (mostly mitral) → RHD.
Major signs (Jones): carditis, migrating polyarthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules.
Prevention is the key nursing role: treat sore throat with penicillin; after rheumatic fever give benzathine penicillin every 3–4 weeks for years.
Infective endocarditis: fever + new or changed murmur in a person with damaged valves, IV drug use or a prosthetic valve.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Splinter hemorrhages under nails, tender finger nodules (Osler), painless palm spots (Janeway), retinal spots (Roth) → infective endocarditis.
Fever + new murmur + emboli (stroke, blood in urine) → endocarditis.
Endocarditis: take blood cultures BEFORE starting antibiotics.
IV antibiotics for 4–6 weeks; complete the full course.
Rheumatic fever: bed rest during carditis, aspirin for joints, penicillin.
Teach patients with valve disease to tell the dentist; good oral hygiene.
A patient with RHD has fever for 2 weeks, a changed murmur and splinter hemorrhages. What should the nurse do before the first antibiotic dose?
a. Give paracetamol and wait ✗: delays diagnosis and treatment.
b. Draw blood cultures ✓: cultures before antibiotics identify the organism.
c. Start oral antibiotics at home ✗: endocarditis needs IV antibiotics.
d. Schedule dental extraction ✗: not before infection is controlled.

notes.title: Pericarditis and cardiac tamponade

lines.text: A patient after a viral illness has sharp chest pain that is worse lying down and when breathing in, and better sitting up and leaning forward.
Sharp pain worse lying flat and on inspiration, relieved leaning forward + friction rub → pericarditis.
Fluid collecting around the heart compresses it → cardiac tamponade: an emergency.
Beck's triad: low BP + distended neck veins + muffled heart sounds → tamponade.
BP drops more than 10 mmHg when breathing in → pulsus paradoxus, seen in tamponade.
Pericarditis: position sitting up leaning forward; NSAIDs/aspirin for pain and inflammation.
Tamponade: call the doctor immediately, prepare for pericardiocentesis (needle drainage), oxygen, IV fluids.
After pericardiocentesis: watch for returning signs of tamponade.
Pericarditis pain is sharp and positional; MI pain is crushing and not changed by position.
Tamponade is one of the causes of PEA and obstructive shock.
After chest trauma a patient has BP 80/60, distended neck veins and very faint heart sounds. What is the most likely problem?
a. Hypovolemic shock ✗: neck veins would be flat, not distended.
b. Cardiac tamponade ✓: Beck's triad: low BP, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds.
c. Left heart failure ✗: would show lung crackles, not muffled sounds.
d. Pneumonia ✗: fever and cough, not this triad.

notes.title: Myocarditis and cardiomyopathy

lines.text: A 35-year-old heavy drinker has progressive breathlessness, edema and a very enlarged heart on X-ray.
Myocarditis: inflammation of heart muscle, often after a viral infection; can cause heart failure and arrhythmias.
Dilated cardiomyopathy: big weak ventricles → heart failure. Causes include alcohol, pregnancy (peripartum), viral infection.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: thick stiff muscle; can cause sudden death in young athletes during exertion.
Restrictive cardiomyopathy: stiff walls that do not fill → right-sided failure signs.
Treat like heart failure: rest, oxygen, salt restriction, diuretics, ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers.
Myocarditis: bed rest to lower heart workload; avoid strenuous activity for months.
Teach to stop alcohol in alcoholic cardiomyopathy.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: avoid dehydration and strenuous exercise; digoxin and nitrates can worsen it.
A young athlete with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy asks about returning to football. What should the nurse teach?
a. Start intense training to strengthen the heart ✗: strenuous exertion can trigger sudden death.
b. Avoid strenuous competitive sports ✓: exertion is the main trigger of sudden death in HCM.
c. Take digoxin before games ✗: digoxin can worsen outflow obstruction.
d. Limit water intake during exercise ✗: dehydration worsens obstruction.

notes.title: Hypertension: diagnosis and long-term care

lines.text: A 50-year-old obese man has BP 150/96 at two separate visits. He feels well.
Hypertension = BP 140/90 or above on two or more readings at different visits.
One high reading is not enough: repeat after rest; use the right cuff size.
Usually no symptoms → "silent killer"; headache, nosebleed, blurred vision are late signs.
Primary (essential) = no cause found (most adults). Secondary = has a cause, usually kidney disease (most children).
Start with lifestyle change; add drugs if BP stays high or organs are damaged.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Target organ damage: heart (LVH, MI, heart failure), brain (stroke), kidney (rising creatinine, protein in urine), eyes (retinopathy).
Papilledema, retinal hemorrhage, BP above 180/120 → malignant hypertension.
Lifestyle: lose weight, salt below 5 g/day, DASH diet (fruits, vegetables, low fat), exercise 30 min daily, stop smoking, limit alcohol.
Drugs: thiazide diuretic, ACE inhibitor (captopril, enalapril), calcium channel blocker (amlodipine, nifedipine), beta-blocker.
Teach: take drugs daily even when feeling well; never stop suddenly (rebound crisis).
Rise slowly from lying to standing: drugs can cause postural hypotension.
Normal below 120/80; stage 1: 140–159 / 90–99; stage 2: 160 / 100 and above.
Weight loss lowers BP 5–20 mmHg per 10 kg; DASH diet 8–14; salt reduction 2–8; exercise 4–9.
ACE inhibitors: dry cough and raised potassium; never in pregnancy.
Beta-blockers: avoid in asthma; they can hide hypoglycemia in diabetics.
A patient newly diagnosed with hypertension says he will stop his tablets when his headache goes away. What should the nurse teach?
a. Stopping is fine once symptoms go ✗: hypertension is usually silent; symptoms do not show BP control.
b. Continue the drug daily even when feeling well; stopping suddenly can cause a crisis ✓: lifelong control prevents stroke, MI and kidney damage.
c. Take the tablet only when BP is very high ✗: intermittent use leaves BP uncontrolled.
d. Double the dose when headache occurs ✗: unsafe; dose changes are made by the prescriber.

notes.title: Hypertensive crisis: emergency vs urgency

lines.text: A known hypertensive who stopped his medication has BP 220/130, severe headache, confusion and blurred vision.
Very high BP + organ damage (confusion, chest pain, stroke signs, pulmonary edema, kidney failure) → hypertensive EMERGENCY: lower within minutes to hours with IV drugs.
Very high BP without organ damage → hypertensive URGENCY: lower over hours to days with oral drugs.
Common trigger: suddenly stopping antihypertensive drugs.
Lower BP gradually: no more than about 25% in the first hour. Dropping it too fast can cause stroke or MI.
ICU care, IV line, BP every 5–15 minutes, ideally arterial line.
IV drugs: sodium nitroprusside, nitroglycerin, labetalol, hydralazine.
Monitor neuro status, urine output, chest pain.
A patient has BP 230/130 with confusion and chest pain. What is the goal of initial treatment?
a. Bring BP to 120/80 within minutes ✗: too fast a drop reduces brain and heart perfusion.
b. Lower BP gradually, about 25% in the first hour, with IV drugs ✓: controlled reduction protects organs.
c. Give oral drugs and send home ✗: organ damage means emergency IV treatment.
d. Wait for BP to settle on its own ✗: emergency with organ damage needs immediate treatment.

notes.title: Shock: recognize early, act fast

lines.text: After a road accident a patient is restless, thirsty, pale, sweaty, pulse 124/min; BP is still 110/70.
Shock = organs not getting enough blood and oxygen. Low BP is a LATE sign.
Early signs: restlessness, anxiety, thirst, fast pulse, fast breathing, cool pale skin, low urine output.
Start treatment when you suspect shock; do not wait for hypotension.
Hypovolemic: blood or fluid loss (bleeding, diarrhea, vomiting, burns).
Cardiogenic: the pump fails (big MI) → crackles, raised JVP; give fluid cautiously.
Distributive: vessels dilate (sepsis, anaphylaxis, neurogenic).
Obstructive: blood flow blocked (tamponade, tension pneumothorax, massive PE).

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Flat neck veins + cold clammy skin → hypovolemic.
Distended neck veins + crackles → cardiogenic.
Warm flushed skin + fever early → septic.
Low BP + SLOW pulse + warm dry skin after spinal injury → neurogenic.
Stridor, wheeze, hives, swelling after a drug or sting → anaphylactic.
Airway, high-flow oxygen, two large-bore IV lines.
Lie flat with legs raised (not head-down Trendelenburg).
Stop the bleeding with direct pressure; fluids: crystalloid (normal saline, Ringer's) then blood.
Insert urinary catheter: aim for at least 0.5 ml/kg/hour (about 30 ml/hour in adults).
Keep warm; hypothermia worsens bleeding.
Anaphylaxis: epinephrine IM 0.5 mg (1:1000) in the thigh, then antihistamine and steroid.
Septic: cultures, antibiotics within 1 hour, fluid 30 ml/kg, vasopressor (norepinephrine) if MAP stays below 65.
MAP = (systolic + 2 × diastolic) ÷ 3; keep above 65 mmHg.
Urine below 0.5 ml/kg/hour → poor kidney perfusion.
A trauma patient is anxious and thirsty, pulse 118/min, BP 112/72, urine 20 ml in the last hour. What is the best interpretation?
a. Normal stress response, no action needed ✗: fast pulse and low urine show compensated shock.
b. Early (compensated) hypovolemic shock ✓: BP holds up by vasoconstriction while perfusion falls.
c. Neurogenic shock ✗: would show slow pulse and warm skin.
d. Cardiogenic shock ✗: trauma blood loss is the clear cause; no pump failure signs.

notes.title: Blood loss: how much has the patient lost?

lines.text: A woman bleeding after injury is confused, pulse 130/min, BP 80/50, breathing 34/min, passing almost no urine.
Class I (up to 15%, ~750 ml): slightly anxious, pulse under 100, BP normal.
Class II (15–30%, 750–1500 ml): anxious, pulse over 100, BP normal, narrow pulse pressure, urine 20–30 ml/h.
Class III (30–40%, 1500–2000 ml): confused, pulse over 120, BP falls, urine 5–15 ml/h → needs blood.
Class IV (over 40%, over 2000 ml): lethargic, pulse over 140, severe hypotension, no urine → blood and surgery now.
Blood volume: adult 60–70 ml/kg; child 70–80 ml/kg; newborn 85–90 ml/kg.
Healthy adults can lose up to 20% before signs show; BP falls only after about 30% loss.
Class I–II: crystalloid. Class III: crystalloid + blood. Class IV: blood + stop the bleeding surgically.
Watch response: pulse, BP, mental state, capillary refill, urine output.
A 70 kg adult injured in an accident is confused, pulse 125/min, BP 85/55, urine 10 ml/hour. Which class of hemorrhage is this?
a. Class I ✗: pulse would be under 100 with normal BP.
b. Class II ✗: BP is still normal in class II.
c. Class III ✓: confusion, pulse over 120, falling BP, urine 5–15 ml/h: 30–40% loss.
d. No hemorrhage ✗: the signs clearly show major blood loss.

notes.title: DVT, phlebitis and the risk of pulmonary embolism

lines.text: Five days after hip surgery, a patient has a swollen, warm, painful left calf. The left calf is 3 cm bigger than the right.
Three causes (Virchow): slow blood flow (bed rest, surgery, pregnancy), vessel wall injury, blood that clots easily (cancer, oral contraceptives).
One leg swollen, warm, tender → suspect DVT; confirm with Doppler ultrasound.
Homans' sign is not reliable.
Sudden breathlessness, chest pain, fast pulse, coughing blood → the clot moved to the lungs (pulmonary embolism): emergency.
Bed rest at first, elevate the leg above heart level, warm moist compresses.
Anticoagulant: heparin or LMWH, then warfarin; watch for bleeding (gums, urine, stool).
Prevention after surgery: early walking, leg exercises, compression stockings, LMWH.
IV site phlebitis (red, warm, tender along the vein): remove the cannula, re-site, warm compress.
Heparin is monitored with aPTT (antidote: protamine sulfate); warfarin with PT/INR, target usually 2–3 (antidote: vitamin K).
Thrombolysis works best within 5 days of symptom onset.
Never massage a leg with DVT: it can dislodge the clot.
Do not flush an IV line that shows thrombophlebitis.
A post-operative patient has a swollen, tender left calf. Which nursing action is contraindicated?
a. Elevating the leg ✗: reduces swelling; this is correct care.
b. Massaging the calf ✓: can dislodge the clot and cause pulmonary embolism.
c. Giving ordered heparin ✗: standard treatment for DVT.
d. Monitoring for chest pain and dyspnea ✗: detects pulmonary embolism early.

notes.title: Aneurysm and varicose veins

lines.text: A 70-year-old hypertensive smoker has a pulsating mass in the abdomen and vague back pain.
Abdominal aortic aneurysm: pulsating abdominal mass with a bruit; often no symptoms until it leaks.
Sudden severe back or abdominal pain + falling BP + fast pulse → rupture: emergency surgery.
Varicose veins: twisted, dilated superficial leg veins from weak valves; worse with standing, pregnancy, obesity.
Aneurysm: control BP, do not palpate deeply, prepare for surgery or endovascular graft.
Varicose veins: elevate legs, compression stockings, avoid standing long or crossing legs, walk regularly.
A patient with a known abdominal aortic aneurysm suddenly has severe back pain, BP 80/50 and pulse 130. What is happening?
a. Muscle strain ✗: would not cause shock.
b. Aneurysm rupture ✓: sudden pain with shock means bleeding from the aorta.
c. Kidney stone ✗: severe pain but not usually with shock.
d. Varicose vein bleeding ✗: superficial and visible, not this picture.

notes.title: Congenital heart diseases: pink or blue?

lines.text: A 2-year-old turns blue when crying and squats after playing.
Acyanotic (left-to-right shunt, pink): VSD, ASD, PDA; obstruction: coarctation, pulmonary/aortic stenosis.
Cyanotic (right-to-left, blue): tetralogy of Fallot is the most common.
Tetralogy = VSD + pulmonary stenosis + overriding aorta + right ventricle hypertrophy.
VSD is the most common congenital heart defect; loud holosystolic murmur.
PDA: continuous "machinery" murmur; common in preterm babies.
Coarctation: BP higher in the arms than legs; weak or absent femoral pulses.
Tet spell (blue, breathless when crying): knee-chest position, calm the child, oxygen, morphine as ordered.
Squatting is the child's own way to relieve cyanosis.
PDA in preterm babies: indomethacin or ibuprofen can close it.
Feed small, frequent meals; watch weight gain and signs of heart failure.
A child with tetralogy of Fallot becomes deeply cyanotic and breathless while crying. What should the nurse do first?
a. Lay the child flat on the back ✗: does not reduce the right-to-left shunt.
b. Place the child in knee-chest position ✓: raises systemic resistance and sends more blood to the lungs.
c. Give IV fluids rapidly ✗: not the first step.
d. Encourage crying to expand the lungs ✗: crying worsens the spell.

notes.title: Breathing patterns and respiratory procedures

lines.text: A patient returns from bronchoscopy and asks for a drink of water.
Normal adult breathing is about 12–20/min; faster = tachypnea, slower = bradypnea, no breathing = apnea.
Cheyne-Stokes: breaths get deeper then shallower, then a pause → heart failure, drug overdose, renal failure, brain injury, near death.
Hypercapnia = PaCO2 above 45 mmHg.
Pulse oximetry normal 95–100%; below 85% tissues are not getting enough oxygen.
Early signs of low oxygen: restlessness, confusion, fast pulse, fast breathing; cyanosis is late.
Before bronchoscopy: consent, nothing by mouth 6 hours, remove dentures.
After bronchoscopy: nothing by mouth until the gag/cough reflex returns; watch for bleeding, stridor, bronchospasm.
Thoracentesis: sit upright leaning over a table; tell the patient not to cough or move during the needle insertion.
After thoracentesis: pressure dressing; watch for sudden breathlessness (pneumothorax), cough, falling BP.
Usually no more than 1–1.5 L is removed at one time (re-expansion pulmonary edema).
After a bronchoscopy, a patient wants to drink. What should the nurse do first?
a. Give water immediately ✗: the throat is numb; he may aspirate.
b. Check that the gag and cough reflexes have returned ✓: oral intake is safe only after reflexes return.
c. Give a full meal to prevent hypoglycemia ✗: aspiration risk remains until reflexes return.
d. Lay him flat on his back ✗: increases aspiration risk.

notes.title: Oxygen therapy and chest drain care

lines.text: A patient has a chest tube connected to a water-seal bottle after a pneumothorax.
Give oxygen for hypoxia: saturation below 92%, shock, cardiac arrest, CO poisoning, major trauma.
Monitor saturation with pulse oximetry at least as often as vital signs.
Oxygen toxicity with high concentrations for long periods: chest discomfort, tingling, breathlessness.
Water-seal drain: water level should rise on breathing in and fall on breathing out (tidaling) → system working.
Continuous bubbling in the water-seal chamber → air leak in the system or lung.
Keep the bottle BELOW chest level at all times.
No smoking or open flame near oxygen; humidify for high flow.
Chest tube: keep tubing free of loops and kinks; do not routinely clamp; encourage deep breathing and coughing.
Mark drainage level each shift; report over 100 ml/hour or bright red blood.
If the tube comes out of the chest: cover the site immediately with sterile occlusive dressing; call the doctor.
If the tubing disconnects: put the end in sterile water.
Tracheostomy: suction with sterile technique, no more than 10–15 seconds, pre-oxygenate.
The water level in a chest drain no longer rises and falls with breathing. What is the most likely reason?
a. The system is broken and must be replaced at once ✗: first check simpler causes.
b. The lung has re-expanded or the tube is kinked/blocked ✓: tidaling stops when the lung is expanded or the tube is obstructed.
c. The bottle is placed too low ✗: position below the chest is correct.
d. Normal early after insertion ✗: tidaling is expected while the space is open.

notes.title: Sore throat, tonsillitis and laryngitis

lines.text: A 12-year-old has fever, sore throat, painful swallowing, swollen red tonsils with pus and tender neck nodes.
Most sore throats are viral; Group A streptococcus is the main bacterial cause.
Strep tonsillitis/pharyngitis → penicillin (benzathine penicillin 1.2–2.4 MU IM once, or amoxicillin) to prevent rheumatic fever.
Viral cause → supportive care only; antibiotics do not help.
Laryngitis: hoarse or lost voice, mostly viral or from voice overuse → rest the voice.
Tonsillectomy for repeated tonsillitis not responding to antibiotics.
Warm saline gargles, soft or liquid diet, plenty of fluids, paracetamol.
Finish the full antibiotic course even when feeling better.
Laryngitis: voice rest, avoid smoking, cool steam inhalation.
Complications to watch: peritonsillar abscess, otitis media, rheumatic fever, glomerulonephritis.
After tonsillectomy: frequent swallowing or bright red vomit = bleeding; place on the side, no straws, cold soft foods.
Why is a full course of penicillin important for streptococcal tonsillitis?
a. To prevent the common cold ✗: colds are viral.
b. To prevent rheumatic fever and heart valve damage ✓: untreated strep can trigger rheumatic fever.
c. Because the infection is viral ✗: antibiotics do nothing against viruses.
d. To prevent asthma ✗: unrelated.

notes.title: Pneumonia: type, severity and care

lines.text: A 45-year-old has had fever, chills, cough with rusty sputum and sharp chest pain on breathing for 3 days. Dull percussion and bronchial breath sounds on the right base.
Community-acquired: starts outside hospital or within 48 h of admission; Streptococcus pneumoniae causes 50–60%.
Hospital-acquired: starts 48 h or more after admission; Staph aureus, Pseudomonas, gram-negatives.
Aspiration pneumonia: unconscious, seizures, poor swallowing → mouth anaerobes → can form lung abscess.
PCP: HIV patient with dry cough, marked breathlessness, few chest signs → high-dose cotrimoxazole for 21 days.
Severe pneumonia (admit): RR over 30, cyanosis, hypotension, confusion, 2 or more lobes, comorbidity.
Mild CAP: oral amoxicillin (or erythromycin); severe CAP: admit, IV penicillin/ceftriaxone, oxygen.
Semi-Fowler's position, oxygen, analgesia for pleuritic pain, antipyretics.
Fluids about 3 L/day to thin secretions (unless heart/kidney limits).
Deep breathing, coughing, chest physiotherapy; oral care after sputum.
Collect sputum for culture BEFORE starting antibiotics, early morning.
Prevention: pneumococcal vaccine, turning bed-bound patients, early walking, suction unconscious patients.
Elderly patients may show only confusion and no fever.
Complications: pleural effusion, empyema, lung abscess, sepsis.
A pneumonia patient has RR 34/min, BP 85/50 and new confusion. What is the best decision?
a. Treat at home with oral amoxicillin ✗: these are markers of severe pneumonia.
b. Admit as severe pneumonia for IV antibiotics and oxygen ✓: RR over 30, hypotension and confusion mean severe disease.
c. Give cough syrup and review in a week ✗: dangerous delay.
d. Start TB treatment immediately ✗: acute picture fits bacterial pneumonia.

notes.title: Atelectasis, lung abscess and bronchiectasis

lines.text: On day 2 after abdominal surgery a patient who refuses to move or cough has fever, fast breathing and decreased breath sounds at the bases.
Atelectasis = collapse of alveoli; most common early complication after surgery (pain → shallow breathing → mucus plugs).
Prevent it: deep breathing, coughing, incentive spirometry, turning, early walking, good pain control.
Lung abscess: pus in the lung, usually after aspiration → large amounts of foul-smelling sputum, fever, weight loss.
Lung abscess needs long antibiotics (about 6 weeks) plus postural drainage.
Bronchiectasis: permanently widened bronchi after childhood infections (measles, TB) → daily large volumes of purulent sputum, hemoptysis.
Postural drainage: position so the affected lobe drains downward; 2–4 times daily, before meals and at bedtime, not after meals.
Upper lobes drain sitting up; lower lobes drain head-down.
After drainage: cough, mouth care, rest; watch colour and pulse.
High-protein, high-calorie diet; plenty of fluids.
When is the best time to do postural drainage?
a. Right after meals ✗: causes vomiting and aspiration.
b. Before meals and at bedtime ✓: empty stomach, and clears secretions before sleep.
c. Only at night ✗: usually needed 2–4 times daily.
d. Only when fever is high ✗: it is part of daily routine care.

notes.title: COPD: chronic bronchitis and emphysema

lines.text: A 65-year-old smoker has a barrel chest, thin body, breathes through pursed lips, and has had a productive cough every winter for years.
Chronic bronchitis: productive cough for 3 months a year for 2 consecutive years.
Emphysema: alveoli destroyed, lungs lose elasticity, air trapped → barrel chest, hyper-resonance, reduced breath sounds; irreversible.
Smoking is the main cause; infections cause flare-ups (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae).
Many COPD patients breathe because of low oxygen: high-flow oxygen can make them drowsy (CO2 retention). Give low-flow oxygen (1–2 L/min nasal), target 88–92%.
Stop smoking: the single most important step.
Bronchodilators (salbutamol inhaler), antibiotics early for infection.
Teach pursed-lip breathing (in through nose, out slowly through pursed lips) and diaphragmatic breathing.
High Fowler's or leaning forward on a table; fluids to thin secretions; postural drainage.
Small frequent high-calorie meals; rest between activities; gradual exercise.
Avoid sedatives and narcotics (depress breathing).
Complications: cor pulmonale (right heart failure), pneumothorax, respiratory failure, polycythemia.
A COPD patient receiving oxygen at 6 L/min by mask becomes drowsy and his breathing slows. What should the nurse do?
a. Increase oxygen to 10 L/min ✗: more oxygen worsens CO2 retention.
b. Reduce to low-flow controlled oxygen and notify the doctor ✓: high oxygen removed his drive to breathe; target 88–92%.
c. Give a sedative so he can rest ✗: sedatives further depress breathing.
d. Lay him flat ✗: worsens breathing.

notes.title: Lung cancer

lines.text: A 60-year-old long-term smoker has a persistent cough, blood-streaked sputum and weight loss.
Smoking is the main risk: about 10 times higher; also second-hand smoke, asbestos, pollution, previous TB.
Signs: persistent or changed cough, hemoptysis, wheeze, breathlessness; chest pain is late.
Diagnosis: chest X-ray, sputum cytology, bronchoscopy, biopsy.
Treatment: surgery, radiation, chemotherapy.
Clear secretions, deep breathing, oxygen, pain relief, emotional support.
Which is the most important way to prevent lung cancer?
a. Avoid cold weather ✗: not a cause.
b. Stop or never start smoking ✓: smoking is the leading cause.
c. Take antibiotics yearly ✗: no preventive role.
d. Drink more milk ✗: no effect.

notes.title: Pleurisy, pleural effusion and empyema

lines.text: A patient with pneumonia now has breathlessness, dull percussion and absent breath sounds over the lower right chest.
Pleurisy: sharp knife-like pain on breathing in or coughing + friction rub.
Pleural effusion: fluid in the pleural space → breathlessness, dull percussion, reduced breath sounds and tactile fremitus.
Causes: infection (pneumonia, TB), heart failure, cancer, trauma.
Empyema: pus in the pleural space → fever, night sweats, weight loss; needs drainage plus antibiotics for 4–6 weeks.
Pleurisy: lie on the AFFECTED side to splint the chest; splint with a pillow when coughing; analgesics.
Effusion: thoracentesis to remove fluid and send for analysis (cells, culture, AFB, cytology).
Empyema: chest tube drainage with water-seal; aseptic dressing care; breathing exercises.
A patient with pleurisy has sharp pain on breathing. Which position helps most?
a. Lying on the unaffected side ✗: lets the painful side move more.
b. Lying on the affected side ✓: splints the chest wall and reduces pleural stretching.
c. Flat on the back with no pillow ✗: does not limit painful movement.
d. Prone position ✗: not used for pleurisy.

notes.title: Pulmonary embolism: sudden breathlessness after immobility

lines.text: Three days after a cesarean section, a woman suddenly has chest pain, breathlessness, fast pulse and coughs blood-stained sputum.
A clot (usually from leg veins) blocks the pulmonary artery.
Risk: immobility, surgery, postpartum, pregnancy, oral contraceptives, varicose veins, long sitting.
Sudden chest pain (most common) + sudden breathlessness + fast breathing + fast pulse ± hemoptysis, anxiety.
Can cause sudden death.
Sit the patient up, give oxygen, call for help, IV access.
Heparin: bolus then continuous infusion; thrombolysis for massive PE.
Prevention: early walking, leg exercises, compression stockings, no leg crossing, anticoagulants for high-risk patients.
A post-operative patient suddenly develops chest pain, breathlessness, RR 32 and pulse 120. What should the nurse suspect first?
a. Pulmonary embolism ✓: sudden chest pain and dyspnea after surgery is classic.
b. Atelectasis ✗: develops gradually with fever, not sudden.
c. Asthma ✗: would show wheeze and history.
d. Anxiety ✗: dangerous to assume without ruling out PE.

notes.title: Chest trauma: pneumothorax and hemothorax

lines.text: After a stab wound to the chest, a man is very breathless, his trachea is pushed to the left, neck veins are distended, BP is falling and there are no breath sounds on the right.
Pneumothorax: air in the pleural space → lung collapses: sudden sharp chest pain, breathlessness, absent breath sounds, hyper-resonance.
Open (sucking) chest wound: air enters through the chest wall.
Tension pneumothorax: air enters but cannot leave → trachea shifts AWAY, neck veins distend, BP falls → life-threatening.
Hemothorax: blood in the pleural space → breathlessness + signs of hypovolemic shock + dull percussion.
ABC: open airway, oxygen, control bleeding, two IV lines, treat shock.
Tension pneumothorax: immediate needle decompression in the 2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line, then chest tube.
Sucking wound: cover with a sterile occlusive dressing taped on 3 sides (lets air out, not in).
Hemothorax: chest tube in the 4th–6th intercostal space, mid-axillary line.
A trauma patient has severe dyspnea, tracheal deviation to the opposite side, distended neck veins and hypotension. What is the immediate intervention?
a. Chest X-ray before any treatment ✗: delay can be fatal; this is a clinical diagnosis.
b. Needle decompression of the affected side ✓: releases trapped air and restores circulation.
c. Give IV fluids only ✗: does not relieve the pressure on the heart.
d. Lay the patient flat and observe ✗: the patient will deteriorate.

notes.title: Tuberculosis: who has it and how to confirm

lines.text: A 30-year-old has cough for 3 weeks, evening fevers, night sweats and weight loss.
Cough for 2 weeks or more → presumptive TB: test sputum.
Spread by airborne droplets when coughing, sneezing, talking; also raw milk (M. bovis).
Latent TB: infected, no symptoms, not infectious. Active TB: sick and infectious.
Only 5–10% of infected people get active disease; HIV is the strongest risk.
Diagnosis: sputum (GeneXpert/AFB smear), chest X-ray (upper lobe cavity), culture; biopsy for extrapulmonary TB.
New patient: never treated or treated under 4 weeks. Relapse: cured before, positive again.
Every TB patient is tested for HIV; every HIV patient is screened for TB.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Painless neck lymph nodes that drain pus → TB lymphadenitis.
Headache, fever, neck stiffness developing over weeks → TB meningitis.
Early morning sputum, deep cough (not saliva), in the open air or ventilated area.
Tuberculin skin test: 0.1 ml PPD intradermally, read induration at 48–72 hours.
Infection control: cough etiquette, mask for patient, open windows; N95 for staff in high-risk areas.
Which finding best indicates that a person needs testing for pulmonary TB?
a. Cough for 3 days with runny nose ✗: short cough with cold symptoms is usually viral.
b. Cough for 2 weeks or more with night sweats and weight loss ✓: classic presumptive TB.
c. Sharp pain after a rib injury ✗: trauma, not TB.
d. Wheezing after exercise ✗: suggests asthma.

notes.title: TB treatment: regimen, DOT and side effects

lines.text: A newly diagnosed TB patient asks why his urine turned orange and how long treatment lasts.
New patient regimen: 2RHZE / 4RH → 2 months rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, then 4 months rifampicin + isoniazid.
Treatment is directly observed (DOT): someone watches each dose.
Missing doses → drug resistance. MDR-TB = resistant to both isoniazid and rifampicin; needs long second-line treatment.
Previously treated patients: test for drug resistance (GeneXpert/DST) before choosing the regimen.
TB-HIV: start TB treatment first, then ART within 2 weeks (delay 4–8 weeks in TB meningitis); give cotrimoxazole.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Rifampicin: orange-red urine, tears, sweat (harmless); reduces contraceptive pill effect.
Isoniazid: numbness/tingling of hands and feet → give pyridoxine (vitamin B6).
Jaundice, vomiting, abdominal pain → drug-induced hepatitis: stop drugs and report.
Ethambutol: blurred vision, colour blindness → report.
Streptomycin: hearing loss and dizziness; avoid in pregnancy.
Teach: take every dose, on an empty stomach, for the whole 6 months, even when feeling well.
Screen household contacts; give preventive therapy (isoniazid) to children under 5 and HIV-positive contacts without active TB.
Women on rifampicin need another contraception method (e.g. injectable or IUD).
Good nutrition; avoid alcohol; ventilated home.
A patient on anti-TB drugs complains of tingling and numbness in the feet. Which drug is responsible and what helps?
a. Rifampicin; stop all drugs ✗: rifampicin causes orange urine, not neuropathy.
b. Isoniazid; give pyridoxine (vitamin B6) ✓: isoniazid depletes B6 and causes peripheral neuropathy.
c. Ethambutol; give vitamin K ✗: ethambutol affects vision.
d. Pyrazinamide; give iron ✗: pyrazinamide causes joint pain and liver injury.

notes.title: Anemia: which type, what to do

lines.text: A 30-year-old woman with heavy periods is tired, breathless on stairs, pale, with spoon-shaped nails. Hgb 8 g/dl.
Anemia is a sign, not a diagnosis: always look for the cause (bleeding, poor diet, worms, chronic disease).
Iron deficiency is the most common anemia at all ages: small pale cells (low MCV), low ferritin, low serum iron, high TIBC.
Causes of iron deficiency: chronic blood loss (heavy periods, ulcer, hookworm), pregnancy, growth, poor intake.
B12 deficiency (pernicious anemia): big cells + numbness, tingling, unsteady walk + sore red tongue. Needs lifelong B12 injections.
Aplastic anemia: marrow fails → low RBC, WBC AND platelets (pancytopenia): pallor + infections + bleeding.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Pallor of conjunctiva and palms, fatigue, fast pulse, breathlessness on exertion → anemia.
Spoon nails (koilonychia), craving ice or soil (pica) → iron deficiency.
Anemia + jaundice → RBCs being destroyed (hemolysis).
Oral iron (ferrous sulfate) for 3–6 months after Hgb normalizes to refill stores.
Give iron between meals with orange juice (vitamin C helps absorption); not with tea, milk or antacids.
Warn: stools turn black (normal); constipation is common.
Liquid iron: use a straw and rinse the mouth: it stains teeth.
IM iron: Z-track technique; give a small test dose first (anaphylaxis risk).
Iron-rich foods: liver, red meat, beans, dark green leafy vegetables.
Rest periods between activities; rise slowly (dizziness).
Anemia: Hgb below 13 g/dl in men, below 12 in women, below 11 in pregnancy.
Microcytic = MCV below 80 fl (iron deficiency); macrocytic = MCV above 100 (B12, folate).
A patient starting ferrous sulfate tablets asks how to take them. What is the best advice?
a. Take with milk to protect the stomach ✗: calcium in milk blocks iron absorption.
b. Take with orange juice between meals ✓: vitamin C increases iron absorption.
c. Take with tea after meals ✗: tea tannins reduce absorption.
d. Stop if stools turn black ✗: black stools are an expected harmless effect.

notes.title: Polycythemia: too many red cells

lines.text: A 60-year-old man has headache, dizziness, itching after a hot bath, a red face and an enlarged spleen. Hct 58%.
Polycythemia = Hct above 55% in men, above 50% in women.
Polycythemia vera (primary): marrow overproduces; spleen enlarged; WBC and platelets also high.
Secondary polycythemia: the body's response to chronic hypoxia (COPD, high altitude, heavy smoking).
Thick blood → main danger is clots: stroke, MI, DVT.
Repeated phlebotomy (about 500 ml) to keep Hct normal.
Drink plenty of fluids; avoid dehydration.
Teach signs of clots (leg swelling, chest pain, weakness on one side); avoid long sitting.
Avoid hot baths if itching; avoid iron supplements.
A patient with polycythemia vera asks which complication is most dangerous. What is the answer?
a. Iron overload ✗: phlebotomy actually lowers iron.
b. Thrombosis such as stroke or MI ✓: thick blood clots easily; thrombosis is the main cause of death.
c. Hypoglycemia ✗: not a feature.
d. Hypotension ✗: blood volume is increased, not decreased.

notes.title: Leukemia and low white cells: protect from infection

lines.text: A 7-year-old has fever, bone pain, bruises, bleeding gums and pallor. Blood shows many blast cells.
Leukemia = bone marrow filled with immature WBCs → not enough normal cells.
Three problems follow: anemia (fatigue, pallor), infection (few working WBCs), bleeding (low platelets).
ALL is the most common childhood cancer; CLL is common in older adults.
Diagnosis is confirmed by bone marrow aspiration.
Neutrophils below about 1,500/mm³ → neutropenia; below 500 → very high infection risk.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Fever in a neutropenic patient may be the ONLY sign of infection: pus and redness may be absent.
Neutropenic precautions: private room, strict hand washing, no fresh flowers, plants or raw fruit, no sick visitors.
Avoid invasive procedures, rectal temperatures, suppositories and IM injections.
Check temperature often; report fever of 38 °C immediately → cultures and antibiotics.
Bleeding precautions when platelets are low: soft toothbrush, electric razor, no aspirin.
Mouth care, nutrition, rest; support the family through chemotherapy.
Normal WBC 4,000–11,000/mm³; neutrophils 40–70%; lymphocytes 20–40%.
A patient on chemotherapy has neutrophils of 400/mm³. Which visitor rule is right?
a. Bring fresh flowers to cheer him up ✗: flowers and plants carry bacteria and fungi.
b. Visitors with a cold may come if they wear a mask ✗: infected visitors should not visit.
c. Visitors wash hands and people who are sick stay away ✓: protects a patient with very low neutrophils.
d. Visitors can share fresh fruit from home ✗: raw fruit can carry organisms.

notes.title: Lymphoma and multiple myeloma

lines.text: A 25-year-old has a painless, rubbery lump in the neck for 2 months, night sweats, fever and weight loss.
Painless enlarged lymph node (often neck) + fever, night sweats, weight loss (B symptoms) → lymphoma.
Reed-Sternberg cells on biopsy → Hodgkin lymphoma.
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma: older people, often widespread at diagnosis; strongly linked to HIV.
Burkitt lymphoma: fast-growing jaw tumor in African children; linked to EBV and malaria.
TB lymphadenitis: painless neck nodes that may form a draining sinus; common in HIV patients.
Multiple myeloma: plasma cell cancer in older adults → bone pain, fractures, high calcium, kidney damage, Bence Jones protein in urine.
Lymph node biopsy confirms lymphoma; treatment is chemotherapy and radiation.
Myeloma: regular pain relief, plenty of fluids (protect kidneys), move carefully to prevent fractures.
A 68-year-old has back pain, a fracture after a minor fall, high calcium and protein in urine. What is most likely?
a. Iron deficiency anemia ✗: does not cause bone fractures and high calcium.
b. Multiple myeloma ✓: plasma cell cancer destroys bone and damages kidneys.
c. Hodgkin lymphoma ✗: presents with painless lymph nodes in young adults.
d. Polycythemia vera ✗: causes thick blood and clots, not bone destruction.

notes.title: Bleeding disorders: platelets or clotting factors?

lines.text: A 2-year-old boy has a swollen, painful knee after a small fall. His maternal uncle had the same problem.
Platelet problem → small skin bleeds: petechiae, purpura, gum and nose bleeding.
Clotting factor problem → deep bleeds: joints (hemarthrosis), muscles, after surgery.
Hemophilia A = factor VIII missing; B = factor IX. X-linked: boys affected, mothers carry.
Hemophilia: PTT long; platelets, bleeding time and PT normal.
ITP: child after a viral infection, well-looking with petechiae and bruises, low platelets; usually resolves on its own.
Von Willebrand disease: most common inherited bleeding disorder; nosebleeds, heavy periods; treat with desmopressin.
Vitamin K deficiency: newborns, long antibiotic use, liver/bile disease, warfarin excess → PT long; give vitamin K.
Joint bleed: RICE → rest, ice, compression, elevation + give factor replacement.
Never give aspirin or IM injections to bleeding-disorder patients; use paracetamol.
Soft toothbrush, safe play, medical ID, teach the family to give factor at home.
Normal platelets 150,000–450,000/mm³; below 50,000 bleeding risk; below 20,000 spontaneous bleeding.
A boy with hemophilia A has a painful swollen knee after a fall. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
a. Apply heat and encourage walking ✗: heat increases bleeding; movement worsens it.
b. Give aspirin for pain ✗: aspirin impairs platelets and increases bleeding.
c. Rest, ice, elevation and give factor VIII ✓: stops joint bleeding and replaces the missing factor.
d. Aspirate the joint immediately ✗: not the first step and risks more bleeding.

notes.title: DIC: clotting and bleeding at the same time

lines.text: A woman with placental abruption starts oozing from IV sites, gums and the wound; she has petechiae and low urine output.
A serious illness triggers clotting everywhere → clotting factors and platelets get used up → bleeding everywhere.
Triggers: sepsis, obstetric emergencies (abruption, amniotic fluid embolism, dead fetus), major trauma, burns, cancer.
Labs: platelets falling, PT and PTT prolonged, fibrinogen low, D-dimer high.
The only proven treatment is treating the cause.
Treat the trigger; replace with fresh frozen plasma, platelets, cryoprecipitate and blood as ordered.
Press puncture sites until bleeding stops; avoid IM injections and unnecessary punctures.
Monitor for organ damage: urine output, breathing, consciousness.
A patient with severe sepsis develops oozing from IV sites, petechiae, low platelets and prolonged PT. What is most likely?
a. Hemophilia A ✗: inherited, starts in childhood, platelets normal.
b. DIC ✓: sepsis triggers widespread clotting that consumes platelets and factors.
c. Iron deficiency anemia ✗: does not cause bleeding with prolonged PT.
d. Polycythemia vera ✗: causes clots, high Hct, not consumption bleeding.

notes.title: Blood transfusion: safe giving and reactions

lines.text: Ten minutes after a blood transfusion starts, the patient has chills, fever, back pain, low BP and dark urine.
Most fatal reactions come from ABO-incompatible blood → usually a checking error.
Two nurses check the patient's name, ID, blood group, unit number and expiry at the bedside.
O negative = universal RBC donor; AB positive = universal RBC recipient.
AB plasma = universal plasma donor.
Any reaction → STOP the transfusion first, keep the IV open with normal saline, call the doctor.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Fever, chills, back pain, low BP, dark urine in the first minutes → acute hemolytic reaction.
Itching, hives only → mild allergic reaction.
Wheeze, low BP, swelling → anaphylaxis.
Breathlessness, crackles, raised BP in elderly/heart patients → fluid overload.
Use a large cannula (18–20 G) and a blood set with filter; only normal saline in the same line, never dextrose.
Take baseline vital signs; stay with the patient for the first 15 minutes, run slowly at first.
Finish each unit within 4 hours; start within 30 minutes of leaving the bank.
After a reaction: send the blood bag and set back to the lab, take patient blood and urine samples.
Transfusion usually considered when Hgb is below 7 g/dl in stable patients; below 6 strongly recommended.
During a blood transfusion the patient develops chills, back pain and hypotension. What is the nurse's first action?
a. Slow the transfusion rate ✗: any blood still entering worsens hemolysis.
b. Stop the transfusion and keep the line open with normal saline ✓: stops the reaction and keeps IV access for treatment.
c. Give paracetamol and continue ✗: masks a dangerous hemolytic reaction.
d. Flush the line with dextrose 5% ✗: dextrose damages red cells; only saline is used.

notes.title: Uncomplicated malaria: test, then treat by species

lines.text: A 25-year-old farmer from a lowland area has fever, headache, chills and body pain for 2 days. He can eat and walk. RDT is positive for P. falciparum.
Fever now or in the last 48 hours + lives in or travelled to a malaria area in the last 30 days → suspected malaria: test with RDT or microscopy.
P. falciparum (most cases in Ethiopia) → artemether-lumefantrine (AL) for 3 days + single-dose primaquine 0.25 mg/kg.
P. vivax → chloroquine for 3 days + primaquine 0.25 mg/kg daily for 14 days (radical cure: kills liver forms that cause relapse).
Mixed infection → AL + 14-day primaquine. Never give AL and chloroquine together.
Any danger sign → this is severe malaria: no oral drugs, give pre-referral artesunate and refer.
Malaria treated in the last 28 days and back with fever + parasites → treatment failure: second-line DHA-piperaquine; confirm with microscopy, not RDT.
AL dose by weight, 6 doses over 3 days (every 12 h after the first two at 0 and 8 h); give the first dose in front of you.
Take AL with food or milk: fat improves absorption.
Vomits within 30 minutes → repeat the dose.
Fever 37.5 °C or more: paracetamol, tepid sponging; encourage food and fluids.
Teach: finish the full course, do not share tablets, come back after 3 days if not better or any time if worse; sleep under a bed net every night.
Primaquine is NOT given in pregnancy, to infants under 6 months, to women breastfeeding infants under 6 months, or with moderate–severe anemia.
Primaquine can break RBCs in G6PD deficiency: stop it if weakness, dizziness or dark urine appear.
RDT can stay positive for weeks after treatment: use microscopy to judge treatment failure.
AL is never used as prophylaxis.
AL tablets per dose: under 15 kg = 1; 15–24 kg = 2; 25–34 kg = 3; 35 kg and above = 4.
Chloroquine total dose 25 mg base/kg over 3 days.
A 30-year-old man (60 kg) has fever and headache; RDT shows P. vivax. He has no danger signs and is not anemic. What is the correct treatment?
a. AL for 3 days only ✗: AL is for falciparum; vivax needs chloroquine and radical cure.
b. Chloroquine for 3 days + primaquine for 14 days ✓: chloroquine clears blood forms; primaquine kills liver forms to prevent relapse.
c. IV artesunate ✗: reserved for severe malaria.
d. Primaquine single dose only ✗: single dose is for falciparum transmission; vivax needs 14 days.

notes.title: Severe malaria: danger signs and artesunate

lines.text: A 6-year-old with falciparum malaria becomes very drowsy, cannot sit up, has had two convulsions and dark cola-coloured urine.

Danger signs: altered consciousness, prostration (cannot sit or walk), cannot eat or drink, repeated vomiting, convulsions, difficult breathing, jaundice, severe pallor, cola-coloured urine, bleeding, no urine in 24 h.
One danger sign is enough: treat as severe malaria even if the RDT is negative, and refer urgently.
Severe malaria is never treated with oral drugs.
Drug of choice: IV or IM artesunate at 0, 12 and 24 hours, then daily until oral AL can be taken (full course).
Alternatives if no artesunate: IM artemether (never IV), then quinine.
Pre-referral at health post: rectal artesunate 10 mg/kg for children under 6 years.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Most important complication to check repeatedly: hypoglycemia (glucose below 40 mg/dl). Convulsions or coma may be from low sugar.
Unarousable coma: Glasgow below 11 in adults, Blantyre below 3 in children.
ABC first; unconscious patient on the side; turn every 2 hours.
Check blood glucose often; correct low sugar with IV dextrose.
Monitor consciousness, vital signs, input/output, urine colour, Hb, convulsions.
Measure fluids carefully: both dehydration and fluid overload (pulmonary edema) kill.
Artesunate dose: 2.4 mg/kg; children under 20 kg 3 mg/kg.
Quinine: never give as an IV push; infuse slowly over 4 hours. It causes hypoglycemia.
IM injections into the anterior thigh, not the buttock (sciatic nerve).
Do not wait for the blood film result to start treatment in a severely ill patient.
A child with falciparum malaria becomes unconscious. What should be checked immediately along with ABC?
a. Serum potassium ✗: not the most urgent reversible cause.
b. Blood glucose ✓: hypoglycemia is common in severe malaria and quickly reversible.
c. Liver enzymes ✗: not urgent at this moment.
d. Stool exam ✗: not relevant to the emergency.

notes.title: Malaria in pregnancy and prevention

lines.text: A woman 10 weeks pregnant has fever; RDT shows P. falciparum. She has no danger signs.
Pregnant women in Ethiopia have little immunity → higher risk of severe malaria, anemia, abortion, stillbirth, low birth weight.
Uncomplicated falciparum in pregnancy: AL in ALL trimesters.
Vivax in pregnancy: chloroquine; NO primaquine. Give weekly chloroquine prophylaxis until after delivery and 6 months of breastfeeding.
Severe malaria in pregnancy, any trimester: IV/IM artesunate; saving the mother comes first.
Pregnant women are prone to hypoglycemia (especially on quinine) and pulmonary edema.
Ask every woman of child-bearing age if she may be pregnant before giving antimalarials.
Pregnant women and children get priority for insecticide-treated nets.
Prevention for all: sleep under a net every night, drain stagnant water, indoor residual spraying, do not plaster sprayed walls.
Travellers: mefloquine or atovaquone-proguanil prophylaxis plus nets and repellent.
Intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy (IPTp) is NOT used in Ethiopia.
A pregnant woman in her first trimester has uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria. Which treatment is recommended in Ethiopia?
a. Artemether-lumefantrine ✓: recommended in all trimesters for uncomplicated falciparum.
b. AL plus primaquine ✗: primaquine is contraindicated in pregnancy.
c. No treatment until second trimester ✗: untreated malaria endangers mother and fetus.
d. IV artesunate ✗: reserved for severe malaria.

notes.title: Meningitis: recognize it and confirm with LP

lines.text: A 15-year-old in the dry season has high fever, severe headache, vomiting, stiff neck, dislikes light and has a purple rash on the legs.
Classic triad: fever + stiff neck + altered mental status.
Kernig's sign: pain/resistance when straightening the knee with the hip flexed. Brudzinski's: neck flexion makes hips and knees flex.
Petechial or purpuric rash → meningococcal meningitis: an emergency, also infectious.
Ethiopia is in the African meningitis belt: epidemics in the dry season, peak age 5–14 years, mostly N. meningitidis group A.
Babies and elderly may show no stiff neck: irritability, poor feeding, bulging fontanelle, drowsiness.
Lumbar puncture confirms it; do CT first if there are seizures, papilledema, focal signs or coma.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Bacterial CSF: cloudy, many neutrophils (1,000–5,000), high protein, LOW glucose.
Viral CSF: clear, lymphocytes, NORMAL glucose; illness settles in 7–10 days.
TB meningitis: lymphocytes, high protein, low glucose, slower onset over weeks.
Normal CSF: WBC under 5, protein under 50 mg/dl, glucose 45–80 mg/dl (about 60% of blood glucose).
Epidemic threshold: 15 cases/100,000/week (population over 30,000).
After LP: lie flat for a few hours, encourage fluids (prevents headache).
Respiratory droplet isolation for meningococcal disease for the first 24 hours of antibiotics.
A patient's CSF is cloudy with 3,000 WBC (mostly neutrophils), protein 300 mg/dl and glucose 15 mg/dl. What is the most likely diagnosis?
a. Viral meningitis ✗: would show lymphocytes and normal glucose.
b. Bacterial meningitis ✓: neutrophils, high protein and low glucose.
c. Normal CSF ✗: normal WBC is under 5.
d. Tension headache ✗: CSF would be normal.

notes.title: Meningitis: antibiotics fast, and nursing care

lines.text: A 30-year-old with suspected bacterial meningitis has just had blood cultures and a lumbar puncture.
Start antibiotics immediately after LP (or after blood cultures if LP must wait): every hour of delay increases death.
Empiric choice adults/children: ceftriaxone (or cefotaxime) + vancomycin; add ampicillin if over 50 or newborn (Listeria).
Newborns: ampicillin + cefotaxime (or + gentamicin).
Dexamethasone given 10–20 minutes before or with the first antibiotic dose reduces deafness and brain damage.
Close contacts of meningococcal disease (household, partner): rifampicin prophylaxis (or ciprofloxacin/ceftriaxone).
Quiet dark room, head of bed raised about 30°, analgesics.
Neuro checks and vital signs every 4 hours or more often: consciousness, pupils, seizures.
Seizure precautions: padded side rails, suction ready.
Watch for raised ICP: worsening headache, vomiting, slow pulse, rising BP, falling consciousness.
Monitor fluids and sodium; watch for shock in meningococcal sepsis.
Follow-up hearing test: deafness is a common complication.
Duration: meningococcus and H. influenzae 7 days; pneumococcus 10–14; group B strep 14–21; Listeria 21+.
When should dexamethasone be given in suspected bacterial meningitis?
a. One week after antibiotics ✗: too late to prevent inflammation damage.
b. Shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose ✓: blocks the inflammatory burst when bacteria are killed.
c. Only if the patient becomes deaf ✗: it is given to prevent deafness, not treat it.
d. Never ✗: it reduces hearing loss and neurologic sequelae.

notes.title: Acute asthma attack: how bad, what first

lines.text: A 20-year-old with asthma is sitting upright, using neck muscles to breathe, cannot finish a sentence, RR 30, pulse 120, loud wheeze.
Severe attack: cannot complete sentences, RR over 25, pulse over 110, peak flow below 50%.
Life-threatening: SILENT chest, cyanosis, exhaustion, confusion, slow pulse, low BP, peak flow below 33%.
A quiet chest in a breathless asthmatic is not improvement: almost no air is moving.
Common triggers: viral infections, dust mites, pollen, smoke, cold air, exercise, aspirin/NSAIDs, beta-blockers.
Sit upright (high Fowler's); oxygen to keep saturation 94–98%.
Salbutamol (short-acting beta-2 agonist) by nebulizer or inhaler with spacer, repeated every 20 minutes in the first hour.
Add ipratropium in severe attacks.
Systemic steroids early: oral prednisolone or IV hydrocortisone.
Stay with the patient, keep calm; monitor RR, pulse, saturation, peak flow, ability to speak.
No sedatives in an acute attack: they suppress breathing.
Non-selective beta-blockers (propranolol) and aspirin can trigger attacks.
A patient in an asthma attack had loud wheezing; now the wheeze is gone, he is drowsy and his lips are blue. What does this mean?
a. The attack is resolving ✗: silent chest with cyanosis is a sign of severe obstruction.
b. Life-threatening asthma: call for help and treat urgently ✓: little air movement, exhaustion and hypoxia.
c. He fell asleep after treatment ✗: drowsiness here reflects hypoxia/CO2 retention.
d. Anxiety attack ✗: cyanosis and silent chest are not anxiety.

notes.title: Long-term asthma: controller vs reliever

lines.text: A patient with asthma uses his salbutamol inhaler 4 times a day and wakes at night coughing.
Reliever = salbutamol (fast, short-acting): for attacks only.
Controller = inhaled corticosteroid (beclomethasone, budesonide): daily even when well; works over weeks; the only drug shown to reduce asthma deaths.
Needing the reliever often or waking at night → asthma not controlled: step up the controller.
Long-acting beta agonists (salmeterol, formoterol) are never used alone: always with an inhaled steroid.
Teach inhaler technique: shake, breathe out, seal lips, press and breathe in slowly, hold 10 seconds; use a spacer; children under 4 need a mask.
Rinse mouth after inhaled steroids (prevents oral thrush).
Two inhalers: use the bronchodilator first, wait, then the steroid.
Avoid triggers: smoke, dust, pets, cold air; treat infections early.
Reversibility: FEV1 improves 12% (200 ml) 15 min after salbutamol → asthma.
A patient using a beclomethasone inhaler develops white patches in the mouth. What teaching prevents this?
a. Stop the inhaler ✗: controller therapy should continue.
b. Rinse the mouth with water after each use ✓: removes steroid residue that causes oral thrush.
c. Use it only during attacks ✗: it is a daily controller, not a reliever.
d. Take it with milk ✗: has no effect on thrush.

notes.title: Burns: stop the burning, judge the depth

lines.text: A child pulled a pot of boiling water onto her chest and arm. The skin is red, moist and blistered, very painful.
First step: stop the burning: stop, drop and roll; remove from electricity source; remove clothing and jewellery.
Cool with running water for at least 20 minutes; chemical burns: irrigate for 1 hour.
Superficial (first degree): red, painful, no blisters, heals in 3–7 days (sunburn).
Partial thickness (second degree): blisters, moist, pink/red, painful.
Full thickness (third degree): white or charred, leathery, dry, PAINLESS (nerves destroyed); needs grafting.
Critical burns: over 25% BSA, third degree over 10%, inhalation injury, face, hands, feet, genitals, infants.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Singed nose hair, soot in mouth, hoarse voice, burn in an enclosed space → inhalation injury: airway can swell shut quickly.
Airway first, then breathing and circulation; give oxygen for smoke or CO exposure.
Cover with a clean dry cloth or cling film; keep the patient warm.
Elevate burned limbs; give pain relief.
Never use ice: it deepens the injury and causes hypothermia.
Never burst blisters, apply butter, oil, toothpaste, creams or adhesive tape; never pull off clothing stuck to the burn.
A man's arm caught fire. After the flames are out, what is the best first aid?
a. Apply ice directly ✗: ice worsens tissue damage and causes hypothermia.
b. Cool with running water for at least 20 minutes ✓: stops ongoing heat damage and reduces pain.
c. Apply butter to the burn ✗: traps heat and introduces infection.
d. Burst the blisters to release fluid ✗: blisters protect against infection.

notes.title: Burns: rule of nines and the Parkland formula

lines.text: A 70 kg man has partial and full thickness burns of both legs (front and back) and the front of the chest.
Adult rule of nines: head 9, each arm 9, each leg 18, front trunk 18, back trunk 18, perineum 1.
Child: head 18, each leg 14 (the head is bigger, legs smaller).
Small or scattered burns: the patient's palm (with fingers) ≈ 1% BSA.
Count only partial and full thickness burns, not simple redness.
Parkland: 4 ml × kg × % TBSA of Ringer's lactate in the first 24 h; HALF in the first 8 hours (counted from the time of the burn), half over the next 16.
Burns make capillaries leaky: fluid shifts out of vessels → burn shock in the first 24–48 hours.
Two large IV lines; urinary catheter: urine output is the best guide to fluid adequacy (adult 0.5 ml/kg/h, about 30–50 ml/h).
Tetanus prophylaxis, pain relief with IV analgesics, high-protein high-calorie diet.
Prevent infection: aseptic wound care; prevent contractures with positioning and early exercise.
Example: 70 kg, 50% TBSA → 4 × 70 × 50 = 14,000 ml in 24 h: 7,000 ml in the first 8 h, 7,000 ml in the next 16 h.
Consensus formula uses 2–4 ml × kg × % TBSA with the same half-in-8-hours rule.
A 60 kg woman has 30% TBSA burns. Using Parkland, how much fluid should she get in the first 8 hours?
a. 1,800 ml ✗: that is 1 ml × kg × %; Parkland uses 4 ml.
b. 3,600 ml ✓: total 4 × 60 × 30 = 7,200 ml; half (3,600) in the first 8 hours.
c. 7,200 ml ✗: that is the full 24-hour total.
d. 14,400 ml ✗: double the correct 24-hour total.

notes.title: Food poisoning: guess the organism from the timing

lines.text: Twenty guests at a wedding develop vomiting and cramps 3 hours after eating cream pastries.
Symptoms within 1–6 hours, mainly vomiting → preformed toxin: Staphylococcus aureus (cream, milk products, salads, handled by a food handler).
Vomiting 1–5 h after reheated fried rice → Bacillus cereus.
Diarrhea 8–16 h after precooked meat → Clostridium perfringens.
Fever, diarrhea 1–3 days after eggs, poultry, meat → Salmonella.
Bloody diarrhea after undercooked beef → E. coli O157 (can cause HUS: kidney failure).
NO diarrhea but weakness, double vision, difficulty swallowing, paralysis 12–72 h after home-canned food → botulism: emergency, can stop breathing.
Most cases settle in a few days: oral rehydration, rest, light food.
Watch for dehydration: thirst, dry mouth, low urine, sunken eyes.
Prevention: hand washing, cook food well, keep cold food cold, do not reheat food many times, food handlers with diarrhea or skin infections should not handle food.
Several people develop vomiting and cramps 2 hours after eating cream cakes at a party. What is the most likely cause?
a. Salmonella ✗: incubation is 1–3 days, not 2 hours.
b. Staphylococcus aureus toxin ✓: preformed toxin acts within 1–6 hours.
c. Clostridium botulinum ✗: causes paralysis, not vomiting within hours.
d. Hepatitis A ✗: incubation about 4 weeks.
